It also explains that PIRLS uses a matrix sampling technique so that each student takes only a subset of the reading items, while performance is placed on a single achievement scale using item response theory. The report does not specify the exact student weight variable names or whether complex survey weights and replicate weights were applied in the Malta analyses; therefore the weighting approach is not fully auditable from the text provided. For analysts using PIRLS microdata, the recommended practice is to apply the PIRLS student/sampling weights and replicate weights (if available) to account for the clustered school sampling and the matrix sampling design when estimating reading scale scores and related associations.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The main study in Malta was administered in March 2016 to 3,647 Year 5 (Grade 4) students attending State, Church, and Independent primary schools. Students were selected randomly from 95 primary schools with geographical representation, with 2,033 students selected from 62 State schools, 1,245 from 25 Church schools, and 369 from 8 Independent schools. The report notes that non-participants included students absent on the day of the test or not satisfying inclusion criteria, and that matrix sampling was used so each student completed a subset of test booklets under test conditions.

data.outcome_summary: PIRLS 2016 is a five-yearly IEA assessment of reading literacy for 10-year-olds (4th grade / Year 5 in Malta). In Malta, the main test was administered in Maltese to 3,647 Year 5 students from 95 primary schools (State, Church, and Independent sectors). Test items were organized into 16 test booklets using matrix sampling, and reading achievement was scaled to a PIRLS achievement scale with mean 500 and SD 100, enabling comparisons across countries and cycles. The report reports international benchmarks at 400 (low), 475 (intermediate), 550 (high), and 625 (advanced), and provides Malta’s mean reading score (452) and distributional results (e.g., 13% above 550; 55% below 475). It also summarizes relationships between reading achievement and contextual scales from student, parent, teacher, and head questionnaires (home resources, school climate, discipline/safety, instruction practices), while emphasizing interpretive caution due to Malta’s language-in-school context and the test-language constraint.
